facts: Australia is the only country that covers an entire continent, and the sixth largest in the world.
Around 85% of Australians live within 50 kilometres of the coast, leaving the interior almost empty.
The Great Barrier Reef is the largest living structure on Earth and is visible from orbit.
AU.about: Much of Australia is old, flat and dry: weathered plateaus, salt lakes and deserts cover the interior, while the Great Dividing Range runs down the eastern side and catches most of the rain. The far north has a tropical monsoon climate with a distinct wet season, whereas the south is temperate, and drought and bushfire are recurring features of life. Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples have lived here for at least 50,000 years, forming one of the oldest continuous cultures on Earth. British colonisation began with a penal settlement at Sydney Cove in 1788, and six separate colonies federated as the Commonwealth of Australia on 1 January 1901, with Tasmania as the island state off the southern coast. Today the economy leans heavily on exports of iron ore, coal, gas and farm produce, while immigration since 1945 has made it one of the most multicultural societies in the world, with over a quarter of residents born overseas.

facts: Fiji is made up of over 330 islands, roughly a third of them inhabited.
The 180th meridian passes through the country, so it straddles the theoretical line between hemispheres.
Rugby sevens is the national sport, and Fiji won Olympic gold in it in 2016.
FJ.about: Two large volcanic islands, Viti Levu and Vanua Levu, hold most of Fiji's land and people, ringed by smaller high islands, coral cays and extensive reefs. The south-east trade winds give the windward side around Suva heavy rainfall and rainforest, while the leeward west is drier and planted with sugar cane. Chief Cakobau ceded the islands to Britain in 1874, and between 1879 and 1916 the colonial government brought in tens of thousands of indentured labourers from India to work the plantations; their descendants, the Indo-Fijians, remain a large part of the population alongside indigenous iTaukei Fijians. Independence came in 1970, though the following decades were marked by several coups. Fiji acts as a hub for the South Pacific, hosting the University of the South Pacific and the Pacific Islands Forum secretariat in Suva. Tourism and sugar drive the economy, and tropical cyclones are a regular hazard; Cyclone Winston in 2016 was the strongest recorded in the Southern Hemisphere.

facts: Kiribati straddles the equator and all four hemispheres, spanning some 3.5 million square kilometres of ocean.
It was the first country to enter the year 2000, having shifted the date line east in 1995.
Most of its land sits barely two metres above sea level, making it acutely exposed to rising seas.
KI.about: Kiribati, pronounced roughly 'Kiribas', is the local rendering of 'Gilberts', and the country is made up of three widely separated groups: the Gilbert, Phoenix and Line Islands, plus the raised limestone island of Banaba. Apart from Banaba, every island is a low coral atoll or reef island with thin, sandy soil. Kiritimati in the Line Islands is the largest coral atoll in the world by land area. Formerly part of the British colony of the Gilbert and Ellice Islands, the country became independent in 1979, and Tarawa was the scene of a fierce battle between American and Japanese forces in November 1943. Phosphate mining on Banaba ended in 1979, and many Banabans had already been resettled on Rabi Island in Fiji. About half the population lives on crowded South Tarawa, and income from foreign fishing licences is vital. The Phoenix Islands Protected Area is one of the largest marine reserves on Earth.

facts: The Marshall Islands consists of 29 coral atolls and five isolated islands.
Bikini Atoll was the site of 23 nuclear tests between 1946 and 1958 and remains largely uninhabited.
Traditional Marshallese stick charts mapped ocean swells for navigation between atolls.
MH.about: Spread across two roughly parallel chains, the Ratak ('sunrise') to the east and the Ralik ('sunset') to the west, the Marshall Islands consist almost entirely of low coral atolls enclosing broad lagoons, with no high ground anywhere. Fresh water comes mainly from rain and thin underground lenses, making droughts and storm surges serious threats. The islands passed from German control to a Japanese mandate after the First World War, and after heavy fighting in 1944 they became part of the US-administered Trust Territory of the Pacific Islands. Self-government began in 1979, and a Compact of Free Association with the United States took effect in 1986, giving Marshallese the right to live and work in the US, where a large diaspora has formed. Kwajalein Atoll hosts a US missile testing range, and nearby Ebeye is one of the most densely populated places in the Pacific. The country also runs one of the world's largest ship registries.

facts: The Federated States of Micronesia spans over 600 islands across 2,700 kilometres of the Pacific.
Nan Madol, built on artificial islets of basalt, is the only ancient city constructed atop a coral reef.
The country is a federation of four states, each with its own distinct language and culture.
FM.about: Yap, Chuuk, Pohnpei and Kosrae, the four states of the federation, differ sharply in landscape as well as culture. Pohnpei and Kosrae are high volcanic islands covered in rainforest, and Pohnpei's interior ranks among the wettest places on Earth, while much of Yap and Chuuk's outer territory consists of scattered low atolls. Spain claimed the Caroline Islands until 1899, when they were sold to Germany; Japan took over after the First World War, and the United States administered them as part of a UN trust territory after 1945. The Federated States adopted a constitution in 1979 and entered a Compact of Free Association with the US in 1986, which still provides much of the government's funding. Chuuk Lagoon holds dozens of Japanese ships sunk by American air raids in 1944, now a celebrated wreck-diving site, and Yap is known for its large carved stone discs once used as traditional money. The capital moved from Kolonia to Palikir in 1989.

facts: Nauru is the smallest island country in the world at 21 square kilometres.
It has no official capital city; government offices sit in the Yaren district.
Phosphate mining made it briefly one of the richest countries per person, then left much of the interior stripped.
NR.about: A single oval island of raised coral limestone, Nauru has a narrow fertile coastal belt, where almost everyone lives, and a central plateau known as Topside that was once covered in rich phosphate deposits. Decades of mining have left that plateau a maze of jagged limestone pinnacles unfit for farming or housing, so food and most goods must be imported. Germany annexed the island in 1888, and after the First World War it was administered by Australia under a League of Nations mandate shared with Britain and New Zealand. Japan occupied it during the Second World War and deported many Nauruans to Chuuk. Independence followed on 31 January 1968, and in 1989 Nauru took Australia to the International Court of Justice over the cost of rehabilitating mined land, a case settled out of court in 1993. At various times since 2001 the country has hosted an offshore processing centre for asylum seekers on Australia's behalf, an important source of income.

facts: New Zealand was among the last large landmasses settled by humans, reached by Polynesians around 1300.
It was the first country to grant women the vote in national elections, in 1893.
Wellington is the southernmost capital city of any sovereign state.
NZ.about: Sitting astride the boundary between the Pacific and Australian tectonic plates, New Zealand is shaped by mountain building and volcanism. The Southern Alps rise steeply along the Alpine Fault on the South Island, feeding glaciers and carving the fiords of the south-west, while the North Island's central plateau holds active volcanoes, Lake Taupō and the geothermal fields around Rotorua. Earthquakes are a constant risk, as Christchurch learned in 2011. Long isolation produced unusual wildlife, including flightless birds such as the kiwi and almost no native land mammals apart from bats. The Treaty of Waitangi, signed in 1840 between the British Crown and Māori chiefs, remains a founding document and the basis of ongoing settlements. New Zealand became a dominion in 1907 and gradually took on full independence through the twentieth century. Māori language is an official language, and the Cook Islands and Niue are self-governing states in free association with New Zealand. Dairy, meat and tourism are the economic mainstays.

facts: Palau created the world's first shark sanctuary in 2009, banning commercial shark fishing in its waters.
Jellyfish Lake holds millions of jellyfish that lost most of their sting through isolation.
Ngerulmud is the least populous capital city of any sovereign state.
PW.about: Palau's main island, Babeldaob, is volcanic and the second largest in Micronesia after Guam, but the country is best known for the Rock Islands, hundreds of small, forested limestone knobs undercut at the waterline by waves and marine life. The Rock Islands Southern Lagoon was listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2012. Like its neighbours, Palau passed through Spanish, German and Japanese rule, and Peleliu was the scene of one of the bloodiest battles of the Pacific war in 1944. It was the last part of the US-administered Trust Territory to become independent, on 1 October 1994, under a Compact of Free Association with the United States, which handles its defence. The capital moved from Koror, still the largest town, to Ngerulmud on Babeldaob in 2006. Tourism, centred on diving, is the main industry, and Palau has protected most of its exclusive economic zone through a national marine sanctuary, while visitors sign the Palau Pledge to behave responsibly.

facts: Papua New Guinea has over 800 living languages, more than any other country on Earth.
It occupies the eastern half of New Guinea, the world's second largest island.
Much of the highland interior was unknown to outsiders until aerial survey in the 1930s.
PG.about: A rugged central cordillera runs the length of mainland Papua New Guinea, enclosing fertile highland valleys that support some of the densest rural populations in the country. Excavations at Kuk Swamp show people were draining land and cultivating crops there several thousand years ago, among the earliest independent farming anywhere. Below the mountains lie vast swamps and rainforest drained by the Sepik and Fly rivers, and offshore the volcanic islands of New Britain, New Ireland and Bougainville sit on an active tectonic arc. The south was a British, then Australian, territory, and the north a German colony taken by Australia in 1914; the two were administered jointly and became independent in 1975. The Kokoda Track saw hard fighting in 1942. English, Tok Pisin and Hiri Motu are official languages. Most people still live rural lives based on subsistence farming, while gold, copper and liquefied natural gas dominate exports. Bougainville voted overwhelmingly for independence in a non-binding referendum in 2019.

facts: Samoa switched to the western side of the international date line in 2011 to align with Australia and New Zealand.
It was the first Pacific island nation to gain independence in the modern era, in 1962.
Traditional tatau tattooing has been practised here continuously for around two thousand years.
WS.about: Two large volcanic islands, Upolu and Savai'i, account for nearly all of Samoa's land, with a few small islets between them. Savai'i is the larger but less populated, and lava flows from eruptions between 1905 and 1911 still cover parts of its north coast. The islands were divided in 1899, the eastern group going to the United States as American Samoa and the western group to Germany. New Zealand took control of Western Samoa in 1914, and its rule was resisted by the Mau movement; New Zealand police killed several protesters, including a high chief, on 'Black Saturday' in 1929. The country dropped 'Western' from its name in 1997. Fa'a Samoa, the Samoan way of life, remains strong, organised around extended families led by matai, or chiefs. Many Samoans live in New Zealand, Australia and the United States, and remittances are vital to the economy. The writer Robert Louis Stevenson spent his last years at Vailima, above Apia.

facts: The Solomon Islands comprises nearly 1,000 islands spread across the southwestern Pacific.
Guadalcanal was the site of a decisive campaign of the Pacific war in 1942 and 1943.
A high share of the population has naturally blond hair, caused by a gene variant found almost nowhere else.
SB.about: Most of the Solomon Islands lie in a double chain of mountainous, volcanic islands, cloaked in rainforest and fringed by reefs and lagoons. Guadalcanal is the largest island, but Malaita has the most people, and the Marovo Lagoon in the Western Province is among the largest saltwater lagoons in the world. To the south, Rennell is a raised coral atoll whose eastern part is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Britain declared a protectorate over the southern islands in 1893, and the country became independent on 7 July 1978. Communal violence between groups from Guadalcanal and Malaita between about 1998 and 2003 led to a regional peacekeeping mission, RAMSI, which remained until 2017. Around 70 languages are spoken, with Solomons Pijin serving as the everyday common tongue. Most people live in rural villages and depend on gardening and fishing, while logging has long been the largest export industry.

facts: Tonga is the only Pacific island nation never formally colonised, retaining its monarchy throughout.
It sits beside the Tonga Trench, one of the deepest points in the ocean.
The 2022 Hunga Tonga eruption was among the most powerful recorded and was heard thousands of kilometres away.
TO.about: Tonga's roughly 170 islands fall into two parallel lines: a western chain of volcanic islands, including active cones such as Tofua, and an eastern chain of low limestone and coral islands where most people live. The main groups are Tongatapu, Ha'apai and Vava'u, and only a few dozen islands are inhabited. Captain James Cook named them the Friendly Islands after his visits in the 1770s. King George Tupou I unified the islands in the nineteenth century and granted a constitution in 1875, one of the earliest in the Pacific. Tonga became a British protected state in 1900, handling its own internal affairs, and resumed full control of its foreign relations in 1970. Reforms in 2010 gave elected representatives a majority in parliament for the first time. Remittances from Tongans in New Zealand, Australia and the United States make up a large share of national income, and cyclones such as Gita in 2018 regularly cause damage.

facts: Tuvalu is the fourth smallest country in the world at 26 square kilometres.
Its highest point is under five metres, leaving it among the most threatened by sea level rise.
Licensing its .tv internet domain provides a significant share of government revenue.
TV.about: Tuvalu means 'eight standing together', a reference to the eight traditionally inhabited islands; a ninth, Niulakita, was settled later. Its land consists of low coral atolls and reef islands with very little soil, so traditional food depends on pulaka, a giant swamp taro grown in excavated pits, along with coconuts and fish. Formerly the Ellice Islands, the group was linked with the Gilbert Islands in a single British colony, but its Polynesian people voted to separate in 1974, and independence followed in 1978. American forces built an airstrip on Funafuti during the Second World War, and borrow pits dug for it are still visible. With few resources, the government relies on fishing licences, overseas aid and the Tuvalu Trust Fund, established in 1987. Seawater seeping up through the porous coral during high spring tides already floods parts of Funafuti, and a 2023 treaty with Australia, the Falepili Union, created a migration pathway for Tuvaluans.

facts: Vanuatu is an archipelago of about 80 islands formed along a volcanic arc.
It regularly ranks as one of the most natural-disaster-exposed countries in the world.
Land diving on Pentecost Island, where men jump from towers with vines tied to their ankles, inspired bungee jumping.
VU.about: From 1906 until 1980 the islands, then called the New Hebrides, were governed jointly by Britain and France as a condominium, with two separate administrations, police forces and school systems. That legacy explains why Vanuatu has three official languages, Bislama, English and French, and why it gained independence on 30 July 1980 amid a brief secessionist rebellion on Espiritu Santo. Over 100 indigenous languages are spoken, one of the highest densities of languages per person anywhere. The islands are rugged and volcanic, with active volcanoes such as Yasur on Tanna and the lava lakes of Ambrym, and Ambae's eruption in 2017 and 2018 forced the evacuation of the whole island. Cyclone Pam, a Category 5 storm, devastated much of the country in 2015. Archaeological finds at Teouma on Efate show the islands were settled about 3,000 years ago by Lapita people. Most residents live in rural villages, and agriculture and tourism support the economy, with kava an important crop.
